title: Variables, data types & strings
summary: Store values in variables, recognise Python's core data types, and work confidently with text using strings.
objectives: Create variables and assign values with the equals sign
Name the four core data types: int, float, str and bool
Use type() to inspect what kind of value you have
Convert between types with int(), float() and str()
Build and format text using f-strings
Use common string methods like upper, lower and strip
Index and slice strings to pull out characters

quiz.q: What does the line  age = 30  do?
options: Creates a variable named age holding the value 30
quiz.why: A single equals sign is assignment: it stores the value 30 in a variable called age. Double equals (==) is comparison.

quiz.q: What type does Python give the value  3.0 ?
quiz.why: Any number written with a decimal point is a float (floating-point number), even if the fractional part is zero.
The quotes make "5" a string, not a number. type() reports <class 'str'>.

quiz.q: Write the expression that converts the string "42" into the integer 42.
quiz.why: int() parses a string of digits into a whole number. float("42") would give 42.0 instead.

quiz.q: Given  name = "Dami" , write an f-string that produces the text  Hello, Dami!
quiz.why: Prefix the string with f and wrap the variable in curly braces; Python inserts its value where the braces are.
strip() removes whitespace from both ends of a string, leaving "hi" with no surrounding spaces.

body_markdown:
## What is a variable?

A **variable** is a name that points to a value stored in memory. You create one with a single equals sign: the name on the left, the value on the right.

```python
age = 30
name = "Dami"
print(name, "is", age)
```

Think of `=` as *assignment*, not the mathematical equals you know. It means "store this value under this name". Double equals `==` is the one that asks "are these equal?".

## The core data types

Every value in Python has a **type**. The four you'll use constantly are:

- `int` — whole numbers, like `30`
- `float` — numbers with a decimal point, like `3.14`
- `str` — text (a *string*), in quotes, like `"Dami"`
- `bool` — `True` or `False`

Use `type()` to check any value:

```python
print(type(30))       # <class 'int'>
print(type(3.14))     # <class 'float'>
print(type("Dami"))   # <class 'str'>
print(type(True))     # <class 'bool'>
```

## Converting between types

Types don't always mix. Adding the string `"5"` to the number `5` is an error. You **convert** with `int()`, `float()` and `str()`.

```python
x = "5"
n = int(x)         # the number 5
print(n + 10)      # 15
print("Total: " + str(n + 10))   # Total: 15
```

This matters a lot later: data read from files, web forms, or a database often arrives as text and must be converted before you can do maths with it.

## Working with strings

Strings are sequences of characters. The cleanest way to build text from variables is an **f-string** — put an `f` before the quote and wrap variables in curly braces.

```python
name = "Dami"
age = 30
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
```

Strings come with handy **methods**. A method is a function attached to a value, called with a dot:

```python
title = "  Data Science  "
print(title.strip())        # "Data Science"
print(title.strip().upper())# "DATA SCIENCE"
print(len("Dami"))          # 4
```

## Indexing and slicing

Each character has a position, starting at **0**. Use square brackets to grab one character, or a range to grab a *slice*.

```python
word = "Python"
print(word[0])    # P
print(word[-1])   # n (last)
print(word[0:3])  # Pyt
```

## Your task

Ask the user for their name and birth year with `input()`, convert the year to an `int`, work out their age, and print a friendly message using an f-string.

slides.title: Variables, types & strings
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One of your path from maths graduate to A I engineer. In this lesson we'll cover three foundations you'll use in almost every line of code you ever write: variables, data types, and strings. By the end you'll be storing values, knowing exactly what kind of value you have, and shaping text with confidence.

slides.title: What is a variable?
bullets: A variable is a name for a stored value.
Create it with a single equals sign.
Name on the left, value on the right.
slides.narration: Let's start with variables. A variable is simply a name that points to a value held in memory. You create one with a single equals sign: the name goes on the left, the value on the right. Here we store the number thirty under the name age, and the text Dami under the name name.

slides.title: Equals is assignment
bullets: = means store this value here.
It is not the maths equals you know.
== is the one that asks: are these equal?
slides.code:
x = 5      # assign 5 to x
print(x == 5)   # True
slides.narration: Here's a subtle point for a maths graduate. The single equals sign is not the equals from your degree. It does not state a fact, it performs an action: store this value under this name. The double equals sign is the one that behaves like maths equality, asking whether two things are equal and giving back True or False.

slides.title: The core data types
bullets: int — whole numbers like 30.
float — decimals like 3.14.
str — text in quotes.
bool — True or False.
slides.narration: Every value in Python has a type. There are four you'll use constantly. Int, for whole numbers. Float, for numbers with a decimal point. S T R, or string, for text wrapped in quotes. And bool, short for boolean, which is either True or False. Knowing the type tells you what you can do with a value.

slides.title: Check with type()
bullets: type() reports the kind of a value.
Quotes make something a string.
3 is an int; 3.0 is a float.
slides.code:
print(type(30))      # int
print(type(3.14))    # float
print(type("Dami"))  # str
print(type(True))    # bool
slides.narration: When you're unsure what you're holding, ask Python directly with the type function. Notice that quotes are what make something a string. So the number three is an int, but three with a decimal point is a float, and three in quotes is text. This habit of checking the type will save you countless bugs.

slides.title: Converting types
bullets: int(), float() and str() convert values.
"5" plus 5 is an error until you convert.
Form and file data often arrives as text.
slides.code:
x = "5"
n = int(x)        # the number 5
print(n + 10)     # 15
slides.narration: Types don't always mix. Trying to add the string five to the number five is an error, because one is text and one is a number. You convert between them using int, float, and string. This matters enormously later, because data from files, web forms, and databases usually arrives as text and must be converted before you can do any maths with it.

slides.title: Building text with f-strings
bullets: Put an f before the opening quote.
Wrap variables in curly braces.
Python drops their values straight in.
slides.code:
name = "Dami"
age = 30
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
slides.narration: Now to strings themselves. The cleanest way to build text from your variables is an f-string. You put a small f just before the opening quote, then wrap any variable in curly braces. Python replaces each pair of braces with the variable's value. This is far tidier than gluing pieces of text together with plus signs.

slides.title: String methods
bullets: Methods are functions attached to a value.
Call them with a dot, like text.upper().
strip, upper, lower and len are everyday tools.
slides.code:
title = "  Data Science  "
print(title.strip())         # Data Science
print(title.strip().upper()) # DATA SCIENCE
slides.narration: Strings come with built-in tools called methods. A method is just a function attached to a value, which you call using a dot. Strip removes spaces from the ends, upper and lower change the case, and len tells you how many characters there are. You can even chain them, stripping the spaces and then shouting in capitals in a single line.

slides.title: Indexing & slicing
bullets: Positions start at zero, not one.
word[0] is the first character.
word[-1] is the last; word[0:3] is a slice.
slides.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[0])    # P
print(word[-1])   # n
print(word[0:3])  # Pyt
slides.narration: A string is a sequence of characters, and each one has a position. The key surprise for newcomers is that positions start at zero, so the first character is at index zero. Square brackets pull out a single character, a negative index counts from the end, and a range inside the brackets gives you a slice, a smaller piece of the string.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Variables store values using a single equals sign. The four core types are int, float, string, and bool, and you can always check with the type function. Convert between types with int, float, and string. And f-strings together with string methods let you shape text however you like. Your task: write a small program that asks for a name and birth year, converts the year to a number, works out the age, and prints a friendly message with an f-string.
